stem.text: Let f be the function defined by \( f(x) = \begin{cases} - 2 x - 1, & x < -1 \\ - 3 x - 4, & x \ge -1 \end{cases} \). Determine whether f is continuous at \( x = -1 \), and justify your answer.

answer_key.label: f is not continuous at \( x = -1 \), because the limits from the left and from the right are 1 and -1.

worked_solution.text: The function value at the boundary is \( f(-1) = -1 \).
worked_solution.rule_named: evaluate the function at the input

worked_solution.text: Using the branch for x less than -1, \( \lim_{x \to -1^-} f(x) = 1 \).
worked_solution.rule_named: left hand limit from the left branch

worked_solution.text: Using the branch for x greater than -1, \( \lim_{x \to -1^+} f(x) = -1 \).
worked_solution.rule_named: right hand limit from the right branch

worked_solution.text: The one sided limits differ, so \( \lim_{x \to -1} f(x) \) does not exist and f is not continuous at \( x = -1 \).

options.label: f is not continuous at \( x = -1 \), because it has no value there, so it cannot be continuous at \( x = -1 \).
options.derivation: a justification about an unnamed it, which reads the missing function value on one branch as missing for f, so the reason given is false

options.label: f is continuous at \( x = -1 \), because the limits from the left and from the right are both -1.
options.derivation: the left hand limit taken from the branch on the other side, so both one sided limits come out equal to f(-1)

options.label: f is continuous at \( x = -1 \), because f(-1) = -1 is defined, so f has a value at \( x = -1 \).
